utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Tuesday, December 9, 2008, and I welcome everyone in the courtroom. I welcome the representatives of the OTP, I welcome Mr. Seselj, as well as everyone helping us. As you know, we will be hearing a witness that has been granted protective measures. Therefore, I will not give his name. This witness will testify today. This is witness VS-1028. The Prosecution has been granted one hour. Mr. Seselj, one hour. After this witness, we will have a court witness tomorrow, VS-044. The Trial Chamber said that after questions from the Bench, and that should take about an hour and a half or two hours, the Prosecution will have one hour and Mr. Seselj will also have an hour. And then we'll end the week with a 92 ter witness. So that's the schedule for this week. I believe that Mr. Seselj has a few housekeeping matters to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have two issues that I wish to raise, Mr. President. First of all, on Friday, I believe, I received an urgent addendum to the Prosecution motion to end the right of the accused to self-represent, and since this motion has 20 pages, exactly, 7.765 words, more than twice the limit, the usual limit, I need additional time to file my response. I ordered Zoran Krasic, my legal adviser, to draft a response, but my wife, Jadranka Seselj, could only bring the response next Tuesday, next week, so I would like to ask for the deadline for the filing of my response to the addendum to the motion by that time. So I would be able to file it on Tuesday. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, since your wife is coming next Tuesday and will bring the response, we grant you this motion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second request, second motion, I did the rough version this morning. I was caught by surprise by the fact that the Prosecution has given me a confidential decision on the actions taken pursuant to a confidential decision of the Chamber dated the 6th of November. I will not now go into the Prosecution explanation, because it is confidential, but the decision that you actually filed on the 6th of November is not confidential. And here it says that you decided to admit, pursuant to Rule 92 quater, the statement by Ljubisa Petkovic. I have yet to receive them. I am actually quite astonished that you have made this decision, and, secondly, because the Prosecution is already acting upon it, despite the fact that the decision has not been communicated to me. I will, of course, be challenging any decision admitting anyone's statements pursuant to Rule 92 quater, persons who are not available to the Court, who are deceased, and in particular persons who are not available to the Court. You had Ljubisa Petkovic here for four months. You convicted him on contempt of court charges. He was in the Detention Unit, and it is impossible to admit any statements of his under 92 quater. If you actually did make this decision, it is contrary to the decision that you communicated to me, rejecting my motion and the motion of the Prosecution, in which we sought the access to the complete record of the proceedings in the contempt of court charges against Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to answer straight away, but let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session. Our witness is about to testify. He's been granted protective measures, so before he comes in, we're going to lower the blinds. They will be raised again once the witness is protected by the screen and has made his solemn declaration. Mr. Registrar, can you lower the blinds and can you fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into closed session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you have already told us that you were born in Bijeljina. Did you live your whole life in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until the war broke out. I worked in Austria for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you make your military service somewhere at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did my military service in Pristina in 1984-1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which unit you were trained at the military and in what arms -- in using of arms were you trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was light anti-aircraft artillery, which is a three-barrelled 20-millimetre cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When did you finish your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1985, the month of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where did you go after you finished your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to my birthplace in Bijeljina. I didn't have any work. I just did odd jobs. I didn't have steady employment in any firm or anything like that. I worked privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, I was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if also other parties existed in Bijeljina at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were other parties; the SDS, the SRS -- the Serbian Radical Party, that is, the SPD, and several other smaller parties. But mostly the main parties were the SDA, the Serbian Radical Party, and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who established the Serbian Radical Party at Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mirko Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know also members of the Serbian Radical Party who were living at Bijeljina at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, when you answer, could you please try to speak loud, loudly, so that the interpreters can hear you. I also noted that the interpreters told me that sometimes you use German words, so please try to only speak your own language, with words of your own language, so that the interpreters don't run into difficulties with words of another language they don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I repeat my question. Do you remember also other members of the Serbian Radical Party at Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember there was Sumar. That was the nickname for Filipovic. And there was Pero Simic and Tuzlancic, who was the editor -- well, not the editor, but he was the head of Radio Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Do you know if the Serb Radical Party had a party office in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it had a party office, but I do remember that they conducted similar discussions in a cafe called Srbija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you also go to the Cafe Srbija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because the Srbija Cafe was in my town, so of course I'd go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you always go there alone or were you in company with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would sometimes go alone, and at other times I would go with other people, with my friends. I was going out with a Russian girl, and I would go and have a cup of coffee with her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was the reason for you to go to the Cafe Srbija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because during the war in Croatia and in Vukovar, when it all started, I was interested in hearing what happened and whether something similar would happen to us in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: For that reason, you had to go to the Cafe Srbija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went for that reason and, well, mostly because the same thing was brewing up in Bosnia as had happened in Croatia, so I was interested to hear the latest news, and I went to see what was going to happen and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you do this also in the interests of your party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working in the interests of my party, but also in my own interests and in the interests of my own people, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you describe us the atmosphere in the Cafe Srbija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already at the beginning, when the war had already started in Croatia, in the Srbija Cafe you can feel animosity towards the Croats and Serbs; total hatred, in fact. And when it all started in Croatia, I think that it was 100 per cent certain that the same thing would happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the war and all the rest of it, and that they couldn't take it anymore; they couldn't take the non-Serbs, because it was only Serbs that gathered in the Srbija Cafe. A long time ago, all the ethnic groups would gather together there in the cafe, but just prior to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were members of the Serbian Radical Party going to the cafe, and it was only Serbs that frequented it in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you realise a kind of hate against non-Serbs there? And if so, who pronounced this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course there was hatred towards the other ethnic groups, the non-Serbs, and this was expressed mostly by Mirko Blagojevic and the other people who led the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did they say what should happen to the non-Serbs if the war breaks out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They said that anybody who wasn't loyal to the Serbs and the Serbian Radical Party, and Serbs in general, would be killed, slaughtered, and then the rest of those who weren't loyal should be sent to -- the Muslims to Turkey, the Croats to Croatia, so that the Serbian part of Bijeljina shall remain ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was there a specific expression for the non-Serbs used by these members of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They referred to us Muslims as Ustashas. They said we were Ustashas and linked to Croatia, linked up to Croats, that kind of thing; that we were balijas, Ustashas, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So also for Muslims, the expression "Ustashas" was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnic composition of Bijeljina at that time; how many Muslims lived there, how many Croats, and how many Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a town, the town, well, in the municipality I think there was 75 Muslims, 20 per cent was Serbs and 5 per cent was Croats and others. The but when I say 75 per cent Muslims, I include the Romas, who were also Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have there already been clashes before the outbreak of the conflict at Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were clashes -- well, not clashes. It's more that the steelworkers were let go who were Muslims. The workers, the editor-in-chief, Jusuf Trbic, of Radio Bijeljina was let go, and other people as well who were Muslims, and you could feel the hatred then, the hatred of the Serbs towards the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what I'm specifically interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please speak louder? The interpreters are really having a very difficult time hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what I'm specifically interested is: Can you give me a reason, how is it possible for you, as a Muslim, who grew up in Bijeljina, where everybody knew that you were a Muslim, to go into a Serbian cafe? How is this possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we need to redact line 14 and after. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: (redacted) everyone will know who he is. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: A while ago, you mentioned you were going there with a Russian girlfriend. How was this received by the Muslims -- by the Serbs? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, this was not interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they didn't like it. That's natural. But I was a young guy, she was a little older, and she was going around with a number of Serbs. She had several boyfriends, and I would go there with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if also other Muslims went to this cafe or worked there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember whether they worked there or went there. I think they did before the clashes in Bijeljina started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So you could go to this cafe without being recognised as a Muslim or as an SDA member; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what did you do with alcohol? I assume that in these cafes, alcohol was served, so what was your attitude towards alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. In this cafe, there were Serbs, and I assume that alcohol was served. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't drink alcohol when I went. I went to have a cup of coffee. I drank coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if also Mr. Seselj frequented this Cafe Srbija when he was in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he would come by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you see him, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see him before -- well, mid-March, he came with Mirko Blagojevic and the other two or three bodyguards or whatever they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you see him also before this, before March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I saw him before March too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interests of Mr. Seselj, I would like to go into private session for my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you remember if Mr. Seselj was in the company of a woman at that time, and what was her name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think her name was Suada. She was a nurse, as far as I remember. I never had any contact with her, nor did I know her before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come back to the first event when you told us that you saw Mr. Seselj and Mr. Blagojevic at the beginning of March 1992. Do you know what they were discussing about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking about killing the Muslims if they weren't loyal to the Serbs, exterminating them, and that those Muslims who remained would be expelled to Turkey and the Croats to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you a bit specify when was this that you overheard this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I happened to overhear it in the Srbija Cafe. I was sitting not far from Blagojevic and Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far you were away from Mr. Seselj and Mr. Blagojevic, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about four metres away. Anyway, I would hear quite clearly what they were talking about. I think I heard it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When this conversation took place, was it in the evening or was it in the afternoon; can you let us know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many persons, approximately, were in the cafe at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that there might have been 10 to 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how Mr. Seselj was dressed that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj was wearing a suit and a sort of white coat -- well, not actually white coat, but a sort of light-coloured formed coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where in the cafe were they, in the corner or in the middle of the cafe? Can you describe this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two of them were standing by the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And you could clearly overhear what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did hear what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did they mention what they would do with the non-Serbs in Bijeljina after the outbreak of a conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They said they would kill them, and anybody who remained, they would be expelled to Turkey, as I said; and the Croats would be forced to go to Croatia if they weren't loyal to the Serbs and the Serbian Radical Party in that town, the town I lived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know why they had this plan or what was the aim of this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The aim of the plan was to cause incidents to break out or to do something in Bijeljina to promote clashes. And an incident did break out there in Bosnia -- well, they wanted to cause an incident so that the conflicts could start in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're talking about plans, so we have two situations. We have Mr. Seselj and Mirko Blagojevic, who are standing at the bar of the cafe, and you overheard Mr. Seselj say, "We need to kill them." That's what you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is the other aspect, the aspect of the plan. Do you think that a plan, such a large-scale plan, can be drafted in a cafe, at a bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that any vital plans were elaborated in the cafe, but what they were talking about in the cafe is what actually happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having overheard this, and noting what happened later in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you concluded that there indeed was a plan; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was of course a plan to exterminate the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did they also mention units who should participate in this kind of cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did mention units: Arkan's units, the Yugoslav People's Army, the reservists, the volunteers, and of course the local Serbs who were in the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your reaction after you left the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went home, of course, and told my mother what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You told us you were also a member of the SDA. Did you inform your party members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not inform them, because I didn't trust the members or some members of the SDA party. And the others, the rest, well, they were normally good people. But members of the SDA, the leaders of the SDA in Bijeljina, were not -- it wasn't safe -- they couldn't be trusted. It wasn't safe to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to other party members later on? Were some lists found, or what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening when the conflicts broke out in Bijeljina, all the lists remained with the names and surnames. They remained in SDA premises. And when there was shooting in the evening, the Serbs took those lists. And after that, after the end of the clash in Bijeljina, when it was over, they went from house to house looking for SDA members. They beat them up, and they even killed some.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you aware if some paramilitary forces were already deployed in the surrounding areas of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan's units were deployed there, I think in the area around the Drina River, Popovi and Amajlije, that they were in the motels there, and that they came into town from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when the conflict started in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 31st of March, in the evening, at about 10.00 or 11.00 -- 8.00, 9.00, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How did this start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the Srbija Cafe, which the Serbian Radical Party had provided security for -- or, rather, they had their weapons there, a bomb was thrown -- a hand grenade was thrown into the Stambol Cafe, and the proprietor was Gogic. Well, that was his nickname. Akmedzic might have been his name. Anyway, a hand grenade was thrown into the cafe, and on the occasion two people were injured. One of them was my neighbour. Can I give his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It's not necessary for me. Can you explain us how did your Serb neighbours react or behave at the day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening, since the Serbs were in my neighbourhood, not a single Serb was home. All the lights were off, and they that gone to their villages, where their parents lived, their family, their mothers, where they were born, in fact; they went back to their native villages, and that means that they knew something was going to happen that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to that topic, let me come back, Witness, to this conversation you overheard in the cafe. It is important, because in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, that was mentioned in paragraph 78, 79 and 80. So what you're saying is extremely important, and it is worthy of some further investigation. So you were in this cafe. You overheard what was said. You spoke about it to your mother, but you did not mention that to the SDA because you didn't trust them, you say. But how is it, then, given the circumstances where you potentially could have been a target, because they wanted to kill all the non-Serbs, why did you not flee immediately? Why didn't you tell your mother that she had to go as well because something very serious is about to happen, is being prepared? So why didn't you do that straight away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I had family, my brothers and everybody else. Why should I leave the place I was born in, why? Just because I'm a Muslim? Why? And I hoped that what happened ultimately would not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But based on what you say, it seems that you heard Mr. Seselj say, "We'll have to kill them, they'll have to be killed," and then the Croats or the -- will be expelled or the Muslims will be expelled to Turkey if they have not been killed. So if what you overheard was indeed said, there's a major risk for everybody, isn't there? Then somebody overhearing this would flee. And you say, no, because you had some relatives. Did you not say anything to your brothers, to all the other relatives, that there was some risk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I doubted that things like that would actually happen. I just couldn't believe it, because President Alija Izetbegovic called for peace, he said that we should go -- we shouldn't go to war against anyone, that there should not be a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. So what I heard, I didn't take seriously enough for me to get into a panic and tell my mother that we should flee and so on. Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you overheard that, you didn't take it seriously because they might have been things you say in a bar? You know, in bars, people would say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did understand what they were saying, but not to the extent that I thought we should flee. Why should we flee, why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you thought that this peril was not imminent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't that great a peril, that great a danger, because the war hadn't broken out yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come back to the moment when the war already broke out or the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how the Muslim population reacted to these first shootings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the evening, and the first shots reverberated, and then a spontaneous group of young men, some 15 or 20 of us, set up some barricades with sandbags and things in the Jugoslavska -- in the JNA Street, Yugoslav People's Army Street, and we tried to prevent something to prevent them from killing our families and so on. So we had a truck and sandbags, and we set up a barricade using that; and we just stood by to see what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You said "we." Can I conclude that you also participated in this erecting of barricades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. I was there, personally, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, so barricades were erected. We can easily imagine how it all happened, but chronology, the sequence of event, is important. Were these barricades erected after the shooting was heard or were they constructed before, which is not the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The barricades were erected after the shooting, afterwards, the next day in the morning, at around 9.00 or 10.00, 8.00 maybe, not even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, the Muslims were a majority, 75 per cent of the population in Bijeljina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many inhabitants were there in Bijeljina at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think as a municipality, it had 33.000 inhabitants, up to 35.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a municipality with 33.000 inhabitants, were there only 20 people to erect this barricade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not 20. I'm just talking about my area, which was called Gozdavic, Tombak Mahala and Hambar Mahala. So in other parts, barricades were also erected, and in the center of town you had the Serbs, the Serbian Radical Party, Arkan's men, and the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were other barricades. Well, there where you were on that barricade, did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes -- no, we didn't have much weapons. We had maybe four automatic rifles and three to four -- or two to three hunting rifles, three pistols, one sniper, and perhaps two or three hand grenades, but nothing much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know which forces -- which units on the Serb side were involved in the attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party of Mirko Blagojevic and Vojislav Seselj, and Arkan's men, the reservists, and even, I would say, the Yugoslav People's Army, who was in the garrison there, in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you distinguish between these different units? And if so, by which way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arkan's men had modern weapons. They were the sort of specials and were well armed, whereas the Serbian Radical Party was also armed, but they didn't have any special uniforms. So, yes, I was able to distinguish between them, because Arkan's men had insignias, had the tiger insignia on their uniforms, so you could see them. And they were ready and prepared, these Arkan's men, whereas Seselj's men, well, some wore uniforms, others had, well, civilian clothes, jeans, the fur hats with the cockades, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you realise a kind of cooperation between Seselj's men and Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Seselj's men and Mirko Blagojevic's men, well, people knew a lot of the local inhabitants because they lived in town, they lived there together with us; so they went ahead and the others went behind them. Arkan's men went behind, because this first lot, well, they knew how to move through Bijeljina. They knew Bijeljina, the town of Bijeljina, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, at this point I would like to have the document 65 ter number 2115 seen on the monitor. And for the witness, it's page 4, which I want to have him shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, what is the origin of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The origin is a book which Mr. Seselj gave to the Prosecution on the 29th of October, 2003, together with 73 other books. That day, he gave us 74 books, and it is his books -- the title is "Serbia's Mr. And Mrs. Caucesku": "On visits to RS and RSK population movements in Eastern Bosnia and in Herzegovina, Chetnik activity in Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like you to read where it starts: "Did you believe that Arkan's influence in Semberija is so powerful ..." Did you find it? It's the third paragraph, I think. My B/C/S is not that good. Please read slowly so that the interpreters can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Arkan --" maybe it's this bit: "Over the last few months, Arkan was really mentioned in the Western media in the context of the war crimes and in The Hague, et cetera. Did you have any specific with the Western --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think it's the second dot which you can see on this page. Could you please read this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. "I think that Arkan -- I think that Arkan had such strong influence in Semberija, that it was so powerful that he came up against no resistance from the powers that be in Republika Srpska, and if --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness obviously doesn't know how to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He read out, "I think," where it says the word is "do you think that," that's the question, and he said, "I think that Arkan's influence ..." so we're dealing with a question, and then there's an answer where as he was reading the question as being an observation because he's assuming and guessing what the text says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Seselj, but I can't read Cyrillic, so I can't understand these letters of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, the witness cannot read Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised about that, because I showed him this document yesterday, and I had the impression that he fully understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I read it again, because the letters were very small, so I couldn't read them properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Do you think that Arkan's influence in Semberija is so strong that none of this is met with any opposition from the official authorities of Republika Srpska, if everything is indeed as you claim?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please also read Mr. Seselj's answer? Read it. It's the following text. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Arkan has no influence there whatsoever. He only took 29 of his men to Bijeljina. Bijeljina was liberated by the Bijeljina residents, and it was our Vojvoda Mirko Blagojevic that made the greatest effort there. Our volunteers were the first to get there, the first to get organised and carry out all actions."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is this correct, what is said by Mr. Seselj? Does this conform with your experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So it's true that Arkan had no influence in the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You say "quite," but not "100 per cent." Is it true? What was the participation of Arkan's men and Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is 100 per cent true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have a number for this document which originates from Mr. Seselj's book.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit number P682.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I demand that this entire text be admitted into evidence, not only this excerpt, because the entirety of the text, I think, fully explains what it was that was happening there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We take note of what you have said. Witness, I'd like to return to the answer provided then by Mr. Seselj to that question. It appears from the answer that the residents of Bijeljina, led by Mirko Blagojevic, have taken over the town and that apparently Arkan played only a secondary part because he only had 20 of his men with him. But after that, the text does continue, and it seems that Arkan's men committed a lot of offences, like plundering. You were on the ground. What was your impression as to the armed force that took over control of the municipality? Was it made up of Bijeljina residents or Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say this? Arkan's men mostly came from Serbia, because I know the Serbian accent, and I know how different it is from the accent of people from Bijeljina. The Serbian Radical Party, with Mirko Blagojevic, was established, and it consisted only of Serbs from Bijeljina and from the municipality of Bijeljina. For the most part -- well, not for the most part. 100 per cent, they were the ones who took Bijeljina, and they were the ones who committed many, many crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say "100 per cent," so you're speaking about Blagojevic's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100 per cent, Blagojevic. Arkan was just an insignificant person. He didn't know anyone there. He committed some crimes on the basis of Mirko Blagojevic, because Mirko Blagojevic knew that if he did anything, he'd be accused or whatever. So Arkan was just an insignificant person there in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you, you Muslims, resist these attacks by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since we had very few weapons, we could not resist these attacks of the Serbs coming from town, and we had our barricades mostly by the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor has just mentioned Serb forces. Well, there's a connotation in there. It could encompass JNA, Territorial Defence, the Bijeljina residents who were a member of the Serbian Radical Party, Arkan's men, et cetera. Those who are the main actors in that operation, who were they? It was said, but it has to be on record. Were they Bijeljina residents, led by Mirko Blagojevic, were they the ones who attacked, or was the attack more coordinated with other individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arkan's men and Mirko Blagojevic's men launched that attack, so it was mixed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now you're saying that the attack was carried out by Arkan's men and Mirko Blagojevic's, and you added it was mixed forces. But in terms of unity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to say -- well, how shall I put this? They were together, they were in groups together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they acted together. But who were the more numerous, Arkan's or Blagojevic's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blagojevic's men were more numerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know to what extent, but I know that we were weaker. I couldn't really count, because we ran in all directions, we were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but were there 50, 100, 200, 300 men? Just tell us roughly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I just know that there were more of them, because -- because we were withdrawing. I couldn't do any counting. I repeat once again, there were more of them than of Arkan's men, because I recognised Arkan's men by their uniforms; and I recognised Mirko Blagojevic's men because they wore jeans, normal clothing, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you already told us that you had to flee. Can you tell us in which direction you fled, and what did you do later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we all fled. I mean, we were all over the place. Everybody fled in different directions. I was fleeing in this direction of my house. I was near the cemetery. That's where I stopped, and other people went in other directions. That is to say, when they attacked front the direction of town. We were not strong enough in order to be able to repel their attack. We were protecting our lives, so we had to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you were at the cemetery, did you observe a specific event, and can you tell us what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw Arkan's men kill the Sabanovic family, and their son -- well, I didn't see the son because I couldn't see everything because of the mosque that was in the yard. They killed an Albanian too then, a brother that I knew, and a woman; and I don't know who that woman was. I cannot say what her name and surname were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I please have the photo which bears 65 ter number 1038 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is this the situation you observed or is it a different event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a different event. On the same spot, an Albanian was killed, the older brother from among the three brothers, actually, who had this "borik" [phoen] shop at the Sabanovic house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: In the beginning, you said that you observed the killing of the butcher. Who is this person lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person is an Albanian. I said in the beginning that I saw two persons being killed; Sabanovic, Redzep, and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is not Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who is this? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I just know he's an Albanian, because he had this "borik" shop there for 15 years. I knew him since I was a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Wasn't Sabanovic an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Redzep Sabanovic, I think that he was originally Albanian, but he's in a different picture; he and his wife, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have the picture 65 ter 1037 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you please describe what we see here and if this is the situation you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is Redzep Sabanovic's wife and Redzep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who is Redzep Sabanovic's wife, who of these killed persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldier's kicking her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which unit -- to which unit these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These soldiers belonged to Arkan's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And this is the situation you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can we please see again the first picture, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, what I would like to know from you, if this is more -- isn't this the same situation, only some seconds before? But, please, you must be certain about this. What we see on the right hand -- on the right picture, is this different from what we see on the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph, where the Albanian was killed, was taken before the other one was, where Redzep's wife is, because the wife -- or, rather, this woman was killed later. This same woman was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move both photos into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the photograph on the left is well known. The whole world has already seen this picture. But on the right-hand side, the lady that is looking after -- caring after this Albanian person, is it the same person as the one we see lying next to the person that is being kicked on the left picture, on the left-hand side picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That lady that is holding the Albanian is standing -- is, rather, by the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see her killed, dead, lying on the sidewalk with the two others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How far were you from this? Can you tell us the distance in metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think approximately about 200 metres. I cannot show it now, because the picture's not there, the sketch. One street goes in one direction, the other one goes in another direction, so I cannot show you where it was that I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were 200 metres away. You heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did hear the shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These individuals that we see standing, three of them, there's three, one of them is kicking the person lying down and has glasses, the two others have black caps. You say they are Arkan's men. We see there are three of them, and there are two that are actually looking in another direction and checking what's happening. When they shot these people down, did they shoot them point blank, without saying anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say whether they had said anything. I just know that they brought them there, to this wall, and killed them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were 200 metres away. You were hidden; I guess no one knew that you were there, looking at everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could see. Yes, I was hiding, but I could see. Well, we don't have a sketch here so that I could show where it was that I was and from where I could see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the person taking the photographs, was it one of Arkan's men, because the person taking the photograph is at the very heart of the action. Was he one of Arkan's men or was it just a photographer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person was not one of Arkan's men, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been a civilian, a reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A photojournalist. Okay. Judge Lattanzi has a question, but do we have numbers for these pictures? The Prosecutor has asked for these photographs to be tendered. Do we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 1038 will be given Exhibit number P683. 65 ter number 1037 shall be given Exhibit number P684. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I did not really understand how much time went on between these two events, because we have two photographs and tow events that occurred one after the other. Could you tell us how long it took from one event to the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that much time between these two photographs, because the first victim was this one [indicates], the Albanian here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I have not really understood. I understood that the person we see in the center of the photographs where we have three people lying down, I thought I understood that the person in the middle is the woman standing above the Albanian in the other picture. Is this -- did I understand correctly or did I misunderstand? Is it the same person, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not understand it correctly. I've repeated this twice already. The woman that is holding the Albanian is by the wall. The other woman that is being kicked by the soldier is Redzep Sabanovic's wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's another woman. Okay, thank you very much. I've understood correctly now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you didn't understand me. I'm saying that the woman that is holding the Albanian was killed, but she's by the wall. The woman that is being kicked by the soldier is Redzep Sabanovic's wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You confirm that the woman we see alive on one picture is dead on the other picture. That's what I understand, but I don't believe that my fellow Judge understands the same thing. So let's be very clear about this. The woman that we see standing, standing over the Albanian man, is it the same woman that we see dead, lying next to Mrs. Sabanovic, who is being kicked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying, "Yes." I would like to know whether my fellow Judge understood that the person standing above the Albanian man is the one that we see dead just a few minutes later lying on the ground, because she has the same vest, we see the same skirt, blue skirt, and there's the jumper also that's blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for our 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Mussemeyer, you have 20 minutes left. We're running a bit late, so please be very careful when it comes to the time you have left. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you already spoke about the killing of the butcher's son. Can you please describe us again in a bit more details what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that the butcher's son - his name was Ado - was running around the mosque, and I just heard a shot and I couldn't see him after that. I never saw him again. I heard that he had been killed and that he was buried together with his parents, in the same grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if the Sabanovic family was the only family which got killed during the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. During the attack from the town towards where we were, they killed a family in Hamzica Sokak. That's what I heard from a man who told us they'd killed a family there, and that we had to withdraw because they were attacking from the part of the town towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You did not observe this killing of that family you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know which -- to which units the soldiers who did the killing belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you observed the killing of the butcher's family, you did not stay there all the time. When did you leave and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I set out towards my house, in the direction of my house. I was running through the graveyard. I heard shots. I heard the bullets hit the monuments, the tombstones. And then I went home, and at that time Arkan and Seselj's units and Mirko Blagojevic's units stopped by the mosque. They didn't enter my part, the part where we lived, and it was called Tombak Mahala. They had already stopped and didn't enter until the next day. And over the radio, I heard Coso Nargalic, who was asking us to hand over our weapons, those of us who had weapons, to hand them over, and nothing would happen to us and that we were free to go, that nobody would kill us anymore, beat us up or anything like that, and that we should surrender our weapons. He pleaded with us to do that, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please specify who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those of us manning the barricades, the young guys who were at the barricades at the time, those of us who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you went to your family house, were your family members still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they weren't there. They had left in the direction of the garrison. It was called training site, Golo Brdo, Poligon. The garrison was called Golo Brdo. And they went there to seek refuge with the JNA, as if they were going to protect them from Arkan's and Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were you hiding in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was hiding in the attic. It's called an attic. How shall I explain it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When did you leave your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left my house when my family arrived. Upon returning from Golo Brdo, my mother told me that my friend, Maida, had been taken out and that I had to leave the house because they would search for me, too, come looking for me and kill me. And that's when I left my house, and I never returned. And while -- the next day, when I was leaving my house, I passed through my road. I saw a white Golf car without a license plate driving in the direction of my house. I didn't turn back, nor did I return to my house. I went to live with my sister in the center of town, and that's where I hid. I was in hiding there for a day, so they didn't know where my sister was. And later on, I went to other people's houses and was in hiding until mid-April. Later on, when I'd already left to a third country - it's not important where I went - anyway, to a third country, I found my brother there, who told me he had been beaten up by Arkan's and Seselj's men, and that they were looking for me. They said that unless he came up with me, unless he told them where I was, that they'd kill him and my whole family. And so he had to flee to a third country, too. He had to pay for crossing the border, I don't know how he managed to do that, and escaped to a third country. They beat him up. He lost all his teeth. They did all sorts of things to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to come back when you went to your house. You told us that your family members already left, and some seconds later you told us you met your mother. Can you please tell us where you met your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day, when everything became calm again and when we heard from Nargalic that we had to hand in our weapons, our people came back from Golo Brdo; and my mother at that point in time told me that they had taken Maida out, that is to say, a friend of mine, and that I ought to leave Bijeljina; I ought to leave town, because Maid was also at the barricades with us that same day. So of the soldiers who came and said they were bringing peace, and tried to enter the hospital - there was a hospital there at the time - they said that nothing would happen, that all they wanted was to get inside the hospital. Well, that soldier, whether he was a policeman who came with Osman before that to try and convince us to hand in our weapons and not to take any action, quite possibly he might have been there. My mother said that he had a black hat on his head and all you could see was his eyes. And so they all issued orders and told all the men to line up in Golo Brdo, to line up, and that that soldier, whether he was a policeman I don't know -- anyway, wearing a cap, he had come in a jeep and he got out, and he looked everyone in the face and watched everyone. And then they took Maid, Maid out, and he was found killed the next day in Sabanovic's cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please explain you think they sorted Maid out of the line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think they took him out of the line because he had been at the barricades and because he had an automatic rifle on him. Well, because he was a Muslim, because of that, because he was with us up at the barricades. And that's what would have happened to me, too, when I -- had I gone to Golo Brdo the next day to take refuge with the soldiers in the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was called then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if Maid at the barricades disarmed someone from the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think he disarmed anyone. I think he took the rifle from this policeman. His name was Rajo, I think. I don't know what his surname was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So when you took off his rifle, he disarmed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was him. I'm not 100 per cent certain, but I think it was him, because later on the rifle was given back to the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already told us that when you left your house, you saw a white Golf coming. Can you tell us, who was sitting in this Golf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see who was there. I think it was soldiers wearing uniforms with black caps on their heads, and they were going at great speed. They were in a hurry to get to my house and find me there, because all the members -- anybody who had been at the barricades of the SDA, they were looking for them. When they found them, they beat them up and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you left Bijeljina at the end, which direction did you go and what did happen at a specific city which you had to pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was hiding, while I was in hiding with my friends, I wanted to go to Brcko because nothing was going on in Brcko at the time, or it wasn't as bad. And I went to the bus station with a colleague of mine to buy a ticket, and at the bus station I happened to see Branislav Filipovic, nicknamed Sumar, whom I've known since childhood, and he was buying a ticket for Belgrade. I remember that very well. And he was looking at the two of us. I turned my head so that he wouldn't recognise me, so I turned my head to avoid a direct face-to-face clash with him. And I bought a ticket that day, and in Brezevo Polje, I heard that the check-points of Brezevo Polje, the control-points there, were manned by the Serbs, and that they searched all the buses. And if anybody was a suspect or was on the SDA list, they would be taken off the buses. I was very lucky at that time, because the soldier who stopped the bus didn't search anyone. I didn't dare look at him, because he might have recognised me. So you had to give your ID card and all your documents if you wanted to cross over into Brcko, but I was very lucky and I managed to reach Brcko. Afterwards, after Brcko, I crossed over into Croatia. And when I crossed to Gunja, I heard that after that crossing of mine, that the bridge had been destroyed from Brcko and Gunja. So then I went off to a third country. "Gunja," GU-N-J-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the document 65 ter number 1052 on the monitor, and have it on page 8 of the B/C/S version and page 11 on the English version. This is an excerpt published by Mr. Seselj in the book "Milan Panic Mora Pasti." That means "Milan Panic Must Fall." It's also from one of the books -- the 75 books which Mr. Seselj gave to the Prosecution on the 29th of October, 2003. And I want the witness to read the two paragraphs from this which starts from the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I have to correct the Prosecutor, because this has happened several times. The wrong figures were quoted. Exactly 80 books is the number I handed over to the Prosecutor at the end of 2003, exactly 80. So he can't say "75" if it was 80 books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we checked, and we found only 74 books. I always had the impression it was 80. Then we counted again and we could only find 74. That is the reason why I'm always referring to 74. Mr. Registrar, could we please have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say, in advance, that in the courtroom I handed over 80 books to a representative of the OTP. He counted the books. Now, where the books disappeared to, I don't know. I'm not interested in that. And I think it was in this particular courtroom I handed the books over. I was sitting in the last row, and an OTP representative came up to me and took over the books. The security guard was carrying the books for me from the entrance to the Tribunal up to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry for the correction, but it was in Courtroom II, and I was, myself, in the courtroom. But I don't want to be a witness here. Is there any problem? Just to save time, can the witness be provided with a hard copy to read from this? Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Witness, go to page 8, where it starts with the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Yes, please, the ELMO. But this is a text in English. I don't think the witness speaks English. It might be necessary for him to see the B/C/S text on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We have the B/C/S text, if it could be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Now it's good, we have it on the screen. Fine. Look at the screen, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please go to 65 ter number 03 -- to the ERN number 0346, and then 3835. It's eight pages later. Thank you. This is the page I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, please read, slowly for the interpreters, also that we can all understand, what is written there. Please read the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The 9th of April, 1992. "Seselj: The Serbian Radical Party welcomes the independent state of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina and will do everything in its power to contribute to its internal stabilisation, the administrative, political and economic build-up or construction, and, above all, to its defence from the Ustashas and pan-Islamist hoards. The Serbian Radical Party believes that the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina are masters of their own fate and that the recognition of the independence of the Islamic Jamahirija in Bosnia and Herzegovina by the European Community does not concern the Serbian people. The European Community can recognise the independence and sovereignty only to the territories where Croats and Muslims live in the majority, and we are not interested in those territories. "The Serbian Radical Party hails the fight of the Serbian people for freedom and democracy. This time again we demand from the Yugoslav Army leadership that they discontinue the policy of waiting, the policy of non-interference. In accordance with the exclusive desire expressed by the Serbian people, we are calling on the leadership so that the army remains in their territory and that it operates as the army of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is the only one to decide to remain within Yugoslavia. The army has no longer a legal basis to consider itself either the Muslim or Croatian Army. "We demand that the army leadership immediately, until the final division, take control over Sarajevo, and not to allow Islamic and Ustasha groups to wander around the capital of what was Bosnia and Herzegovina until yesterday. I think that Sarajevo should be divided into a Serbian and Muslim part."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you for this paragraph. Could you please read the other one, the next one, which is much shorter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The Serbian Radical Party will render all kinds of assistance to the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it has done hitherto. Today's press conference is attended by the president of the Regional Board of the Serbian Radical Party for Northeastern Bosnia, and the president of the Serbian Chetnik Movement over there and the commander of the Serbian volunteers, Mirko Blagojevic. The commander of the Serbian volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This has been read out so badly that I think that the Prosecutor should have brought in somebody who knows the Serbian language and for it to be read out fluently, because what's the purpose of having a semi-literate read out the text who's never seen the text in his life before? And the witness can express his opinion about what was read out, but this way the text has been distorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Notwithstanding what was just said, what is your question, Prosecutor, because two paragraphs have just been read out. What is the question you want to put now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think before I come to the questions, I want to mention that here is no place to offend the witness. The accused is not entitled to offend the witness, which he did some seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: My question is: What was the majority of the population in Bijeljina? Can you please let us know? Was it a Serb majority there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Muslims were the majority in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph is mentioned the decisive role which Mirko Blagojevic had in the takeover of Bijeljina. Can you confirm that he had a decisive role there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did play a decisive role there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P685. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer, your time is up. Maybe time for one last question, but you've used the hour that had been granted to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I only have one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if you think back what you overheard in the conversation between Mr. Seselj and Mr. Blagojevic in the Cafe Srbija at the beginning of March, and what happened later, do you see any connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course you can see a connection, that what they were talking about in Cafe Srbija came to pass. The area was cleansed of non-Serbs, Muslims and Croats, which means that's it. That's what was discussed and said in the Cafe Srbija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Mr. President, this was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, unless my fellow Judge has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, the Trial Chamber, and we're reminded of it by Judge Harhoff, says this: There were two statements, one given in 2007, but there was a former one in 2004, and they're basically the same. Why was there, in 2007, the same statement as the one given in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It was the intention of the Prosecution to get a new 92 ter statement at that time. It was before Your Honours rendered the decision from the 7th of January, 2008, so it's not in the format which you requested in that decision because it was done before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. VS-1028, a few times the Prosecutor asked you about the ethnic structure of the municipality of Bijeljina before the war, and you keep insisting on the Muslim population being a majority there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, the municipality, the town of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. According to the last census in 1991, that was the last census that was organised, Bijeljina had a population of 96 .796 inhabitants. Serbs accounted for 57.551, which means that Serbs were 59.4 per cent. Muslims were 30.314, which is to say 31.3 per cent. Croats, only 517, which means .5 per cent. Yugoslavs, 4.256, 4.4 per cent; and the rest, others, 4.168, which is to say 4.4 per cent. These are officials figure of the 1991 census, and you see that what you have been stating is not true; namely, that Muslims were a majority in the Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You don't want to understand me or you cannot understand me? You're speaking Serbian, I'm speaking Bosnian. I'm saying that the town of Bijeljina. I'm not talking about the municipality. I'm talking about the town. Cadzavica, Crnaljevo, there are a lot of villages in the municipality of Bijeljina. I was talking about the town of Bijeljina. Please, if you don't understand my language, what language should I speak to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You kept saying "municipality" and "municipality," that's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town of Bijeljina, the town of Bijeljina. I lived in the town, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's not a municipality that takes up half of Siberia. It is an average municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a municipality that includes Crnaljevo, Cadzavica, Bijelo Polje. The Serbian majority of villages, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please wait for my question. After the fighting for Bijeljina, in which the Serb forces won over the Muslim forces, defeated them, you went to a third country. I'm supposed to keep that secret. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. And you have been staying in that third country since 1992 to the present day; right? To this day, you live in this third country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in this third country, but I was in the same one all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there were two third countries. So there was a third country and a fourth country, actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Until what country was the third country and from what year did the fourth country start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until 1995, it was the third country, and since 1995, it's been the fourth country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, so you still live in the fourth country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Up until 2008, that is to say, for 13 years, you have been struggling to get a residency permit in that country; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got a residency permit in that country before -- without The Hague Tribunal. Do you want me to tell you why? Because my mother still lived in Bijeljina. That's why. I did not make any statements to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wait a bit to hear my question. When was it that you got this residency permit for staying in that third country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So for 12 years, you struggled before the state authorities of that fourth country to get a residency permit, and finally, in 2007, you got it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. So that's what I'm interested in. And I see here I have some documentation about that, how many times you were refused. I have the reasons why you were refused. And you kept insisting -- and you even got married there. Your wife had a residency permit, and then you tried to take advantage of that as an argument, and yet again they refused you; right? They refused you several times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did get a residency permit. I'm a married man, and I've been living with this woman since 1997, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, you got a residency permit in 2007. That's what you just said yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Up until 2007, you were struggling to get that residency permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't struggling, because in the third country, when I was there, I got a residency permit. So it's not the residency or the permit that matter. It doesn't matter where I am.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I hope you have also received this document that I have. It's 10 pages' long, 10 pages. We see the struggle of this witness to get a residency permit in this fourth country. So if you've already received this, perhaps I shouldn't dwell on it any longer. I hope that the OTP provided you with this, just like they provided me with this document. Could you please tell me whether you indeed have this or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I insist. I insist that the Prosecution provide you with this document immediately so that you could follow what it is that I'm talking about. I think that that is indispensable for you, because this is of particular importance in terms of establishing the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, it is you, because it is Defence that should present this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I got this from the OTP yesterday, yesterday or was it Friday night? I think it was yesterday. No, Friday night. Yes, all right, Friday night, after 1800 hours. That's what the OTP provided to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have to explain this. I had in mind this document. I had seen it some years ago.
