It did not pop up with our normal searches, but I was aware that it exists, so I -- it cost me a lot of time to find it. I found it. It was in a different language. It had to be translated into English, and from English into B/C/S. That needed time, and that's the reason why we disclosed it so late. And the disclosure was on Friday evening. This is as far as I remember. We have it now in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we trust you. There is a document that states that the witness -- it took years for the witness to get a final residence permit. But apart from that, what are you hinting at? Please get to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to put my question, but I think that you have to have the document in front of you in order to be able to follow this, because I have to keep this secret, what the country is, and there's some other information that I have to keep secret. And I imagine that the Prosecution is in a position to provide you with copies straight away. If you think that this is not necessary, I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1028, since eight years -- no, nine years -- for nine years, you had a problem with your residency permit, and since we see here how many times they refused you, and higher instances also discarded your appeals, you complained to different administrative organs, different courts, and this is explained in 10 pages. In 2007, you had this idea to get in touch with The Hague Tribunal and to offer to be a false witness in the proceedings against me; and from The Hague Tribunal you asked, in return, to be helped by them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I believe Mr. Mussemeyer is raising to his feet exactly for that. I mean, don't talk about false witnesses. Please try to first highlight that he took -- he decided to initiate the contact with The Hague to offer his testimony and so forth and so on. So Mr. Mussemeyer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj is referring to 2007. How, then, is it possible that we already have a statement from the witness of 2004?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 2004. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of translation was received. I said "2004." At least that's what I seem to recall that I said, "2004." I'm looking for it now, but it's disappeared, it's disappeared from the transcript. I don't know how a person can return this transcript. I don't know whether it's possible at all. I said that in 2004, the witness turned to the OTP in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. 2003 or 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did you do that? Did you send a letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why are you asking me that? You mean why I turned to them in 2003 or 2004? Do I have to say why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're not here to quarrel with me. You're just here to answer my questions. I'm not asking you why it was that you turned to them but how you turned to them. Was it by telephone, letter, or what? Answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You called The Hague by phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Hague OTP, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you said that you wanted to be a witness in the proceedings against me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, because I had arguments. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say straight away then that you were in this foreign country and that you had problems with your residency permit in that country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that straight away. I said that -- I said that I wanted to testify against you because I had arguments against you, against your political party, the one that you were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I assume that you understand that I'm not interested in your arguments against me. Just give me answers to the questions I'm putting. You said during the direct examination what your arguments against me were. I'm not interested in that any longer. Now just answer my questions. When you first phoned them, how did they react from The Hague OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, they accepted that I should be a witness, and of course they came to examine me in that country where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When they came to examine you, did you say that you had problems with your residency permit in that country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that I wanted to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you tell them that you had problems in that country, problems with the residency permit in that country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I had problems when they already wanted to return me from that country, because I could not return, because it was dangerous for me to return to my country. They kept trying to send me back to my country. Why would I go back when it was dangerous? I couldn't go anywhere, so I wanted to stay in that country in order to protect myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm really not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why are you not interested in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not going to explain this to you why you're not interested in this. Just answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You just want me to give you brief answers in just the things that you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why don't you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't want to quarrel and squabble with you here and explain things to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're not interested in details, and I don't want to give answers then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I insist that you make the witness answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is quite a specific procedure. In your country or my country, things would not happen this way, because in my country, Judges ask questions; and I believe that the questioning is courteous in our countries. But here the Prosecution asked questions, and then the Defence asks questions. And the Defence is asking questions from their own point of view. And Mr. Seselj, with his question, is trying to demonstrate that your testimony, your 2004 testimony, had a hidden agenda behind it, and in order to establish this, he has to put a number of questions to you. It might be very unpleasant, but please answer the questions that are put to you. Please continue, Mr. Seselj, and slow down, please slow down. You're talking much too fast, and the interpreters are raising the white flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you complain to the OTP in The Hague that you had problems with your residency permit in that country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I complained -- no, I didn't complain. I said that I had problems, that "abschiebung" [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the witness lapses into German.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so I didn't know where I could be a witness, I couldn't tell them where they could find me, so then it would be important for me to be there for as long as the court proceedings were on. And the trial has been on until 2008, so from 2004 until 2007. I wouldn't come 2008 if I had some kind of interest between those two other dates, because I already have a residency permit in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. How many days elapsed between your conversation with The Hague investigators and the signing of your statement in that country, up until the moment when you turned to The Hague OTP and when you said that you had problems with your residency permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had this conversation, this interview with The Hague OTP in that country; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the result of that conversation was the statement that they wrote up and that you signed; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say to them straight away then that you had problems with your residency permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many days elapsed from the signing of the statement up until the moment when you said that you had problems with your residency permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. What I have here is information to the effect that you talked to The Hague investigators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Given the problem raised, Mr. Mussemeyer, the Trial Chamber would like to have this document, this 10-page document relating to all the difficulties encountered by the witness to obtain his residency permit, and the Trial Chamber will then see whether this document should be admitted, "yes" or "no," but we absolutely need it. Could we please have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think we have one copy in the courtroom. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The case manager will send it to the court officer so it can be printed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So according to the information I have, on the 24th and 25th of September, 2004, you had this interview conducted with the investigators the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 14th of December, 2004, Patrick Lopez-Terres, the chief investigations of the OTP, addressed the authorities of the state in which you wished to obtain a residency permit, and he says: "Reference our letter from the 28th of September, 2004." So if you talked to them on the 24th and the 25th of September, already on the 28th of September they sent a letter to the state authorities of the said country, intervening in your case. I did not receive that letter. The OTP did not give me that letter. They gave me the letter of the 14th of December. That means that immediately when being interviewed by the Hague investigators, you said that you had a problem with your residency permit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, if you want it that way, but the papers show something different: "And we wish to confirm that the above-mentioned person is a witness in the case of the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. The trial will not start before 2006. What is envisaged is that due to the importance of the testimony involved, this person will be asked to testify in other proceedings before this Court. Therefore, we would appreciate it if the relevant authorities would make an exception in the case of this person and the members of his family, in terms of repatriation to ..." and then the country's name is mentioned, "... for at least two years. If you should require an answer, we can confirm it at any given point in time, whether we still count on this person." So they are asking for repatriation to be delayed for two years in your case; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Obviously, the result of that letter of theirs, you were not expelled from that state. And then in 2007, what a strange coincidence, you sign a new statement for the OTP. I don't have it now. If the secretary from the OTP would be kind enough to find that statement for 2007. I assume that she can do that quickly and easily. So in 2007, you get a permanent residency permit in that said country, and you sign a new statement for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not right. Your Honour, may I say something? Before I signed this statement in 2007, my wife -- my wife that I married -- the lady I married in 2004 was already working full time in that state, and then that state, this town, asked for my wife to work for eight hours; that is to say, that we would not depend on the state, so that I could get this residency. So what I signed in 2007, this statement, has nothing to do whatsoever with my residency and -- well, on the basis of my wife, you can have this confirmed by the state that I was in. I got residency on the basis of the work of my wife and on the basis of my wife, in general. So 100 per cent, what Mr. Seselj is saying is a lie, that it's on account of some interests that I signed this in 2007, so that I could get a new residency permit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1028, do you have a passport on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you show your passport to the Trial Chamber; not -- you can do this through the usher. You don't have to get up, yourself, but just so we can see when this residency permit dates from, as of what date it's valid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean your passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But when I asked you whether you have a passport on you, you said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant I don't have it in the courtroom, but in the room where my wife is staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now you're saying that I'm lying. Yes, quite normally. And the Prosecution -- or, rather, the Trial Chamber won't allow me to say you're lying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just want to say that there was no signature in 2007 in giving my statement because of the residency, so that means your information is not correct. I received residency status on the basis of my wife being employed, so that's it, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, that piece of information, Judges, would be important for us to see this coincidence between the signing of a new statement and the issuing of a residency permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we don't know what country this passport comes from, but are you a Bosnia-Herzegovinian national?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this passport must have been issued by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I assume that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was issued a passport in the country in which I reside, in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Embassy there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a passport issued by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is the embassy of the country where you reside now that issued this passport. But in your BiH passport, your residency permit is not mentioned, because this has nothing to do with it; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't. You can check out, in the country I'm living in and in the town, that in the papers of that state, well, you can take my documents and see on what basis I was granted residency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you state here a completely wrong piece of information, that in mid-March 1992, as you say, 15 to 20 days before Bijeljina was taken, I was in Bijeljina myself, and you link that up with the following piece of information; that three or four months earlier on, and that's to be found in paragraph 18, that most probably at the end of 1991 I went to the same cafe with a certain Suada person. And you say she was a Muslim and rumours had it that she was Seselj's lover; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to provide you with information as to when exactly I was in Bijeljina. I was in Bijeljina on the 9th of December, 1990, on the very day of the elections in Serbia, and I delivered lectures in the Srbija Cafe. They removed the tables. Lots of people had gathered there, and I had a lecture. Did you attend that lecture, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear about that lecture of mine at the end of 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The second time I was in Bijeljina was on the 23rd -- or, rather, sometime in February, possibly the 23rd, in 1991, immediately after the Assembly in Kragujevac. And we're talking about February 1991 now. The third time, I just passed through Bijeljina at the beginning of April 1991 on my way to Knin, and with me were Maja Gojkovic and Aleksandar Stefanovic; and we were joined in Bijeljina by Mirko Blagojevic, and we stayed there for just 20 minutes. That's April 1991. The next time that I was in Bijeljina, according to the official data of the Serbian Radical Party, only on the 21st of March, 1993, when a rally -- a party rally was held in front of the municipality building. So those are official data from the Radical Party about my stays and visits to Bijeljina. Are they correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, as far as the young lady you mentioned, she was my girlfriend until the end of the 1980s, and certainly people knew about that in Bijeljina, because I would visit Bijeljina from time to time and she would come to Belgrade from time to time. Her name was not Suada. I'm not going to tell you what her name was, because that's not important. She was not a nurse. What she was was an employee, a clerk in an enterprise; and I saw her for the last time on the 9th of December, 1990, precisely at the lecture I held in the Srbija Cafe. And you heard some rumours about my having a girlfriend, and then you wanted, in a way, to say that she was my mistress, lover. She wasn't a mistress or a lover. She was my girlfriend. You wanted to berate it all. I was going out with her publicly in Belgrade and in Bijeljina. And then you mixed up the years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't mix up the years. You can say whatever you like, where you were and what you did, but I'm certain I didn't mix up the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, you did, you mixed them up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't mix the years up. You can say whatever you like, give us whatever dates you like and write down whatever dates you like, but what I said is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. It's quite obvious you're telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I think everybody understands that, and it's clear to one and all, except to the Prosecutor. Then you went on to invent that for 15 to 20 days, I was in Bijeljina, and in the Srbija Cafe I sat up in the bar and said how all Muslims should be killed and expelled to Turkey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You invented that. You simply invented that so that in the eyes of The Hague investigators, you should score a point and to have them help you to gain a residence permit in Germany; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. If you say it isn't, let's move on. Now, here in this statement of yours, you present some other incorrect information, from which we can see that in actual fact, you don't know about the situation, you didn't know about the events in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about them, because I am a local, I was a local child there from the town, and everything I said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You spoke about fighting in Bijeljina. You were a member of the Patriotic League, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't a member of the Patriotic League. What I was was an ordinary citizen of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you joined the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never joined the Green Berets, never in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did you have weapons during that fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And to what unit did you belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To no unit. I was an ordinary citizen. We were at the barricades, ordinary citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At a point in time, you took over Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, and then the fighting in Bijeljina went on for four days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long did the fighting go on for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fighting did not go on for four days. They were just in the evening and the following days. So on the third day, the next day, we handed in our weapons, when Nargalic told us that we should hand over our weapons. So the fighting didn't go on. The fighting just went on, on the 31st in the evening and the 1st, up until the afternoon, and that was the end of it. So when I spent the night in my attic, it was the next day that we handed over our weapons. And then Arkan's men and your forces entered my part of town, which is called Tombak Mahala, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, listen to me. I have in front of me Vahid Karavelic's book. Have you heard of Vahid Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Commander of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He wrote a book, "The Aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Northeast Bosnia, 1991 to 1992," and in that book he describes of course from his own angle of vision all the events that took place in the entire Tuzla region. And then he goes on to say the following, referring to Bijeljina: "The inhabitants of Northeastern Bosnia, through the Patriotic League, the police and the Territorial Defence of the SR BiH, and other defence forms of organisation, set up resistance to the aggressor in Bijeljina during the four-day defence of Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct, that's not true. I was in Bijeljina at that time, so I know the situation better than this man Vahid or whatever his name is, the commander. I know better than him. He wasn't from Bijeljina. I'm a local of Bijeljina and a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was in Bijeljina at the time. The war was going on from the 31st, in the evening, up until the 1st, in the afternoon. The next day, the following day, the fighting stopped. We handed over our weapons to the SUP in Bijeljina, and the Muslims were not in the police force. Most of the people in the police and the Territorial Defence were Serbs, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're telling me something I'm not asking you about. Is Vahid Karavelic a general, was he a general? A general of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the Muslim army, but the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You're wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Now, let's see what he says after that. He goes on to say, in addition to saying that the fighting for Bijeljina went on for four days, he goes on to say the following: "The Regional Staff of the Patriotic League of Tuzla at the time, as well as the Municipal Staff of the Patriotic League of Bijeljina were conscious of the overall political and military situation of Bijeljina and the situation in the region further afield. The greatest resistance in defending Bijeljina was put up by the Patriotic League of Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in the footnote on page 236, he mentioned Alija Izetbegovic's speech at the Congress of the SDA of the BH in Sarajevo on the 6th and 7th of September, 1997; and in that speech of his, Alija Izetbegovic commends the Patriotic League and says that it put up the greatest resistance in the defence of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true and correct. We weren't able to put up a resistance in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, here's what Alija Izetbegovic says. He is commending you and says that the resistance went on for four days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true. The resistance was not put up over four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, Vahid Karavelic, on page 236, says something else which is quite important. He says the speedy occupation of Bijeljina was assisted by the psychological and propaganda activity of the aggressor and the antagonisms between the political and military wing of the Patriotic League of Bijeljina. Therefore, he's complaining and says that among your ranks, there was antagonism, antagonism within your ranks between the political and military wing. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you have problems among your own ranks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not in our ranks. We were citizens, and we had rallied together. We weren't a league of any kind. We had no uniform. We were normal civilians, civilians, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I hope you're not angry with me for believing Vahid Karavelic more than I believe you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he cannot talk about things he didn't see, and I don't think he was there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's see what he says further on. He says: "Although the political leadership expressly challenged the military wing, putting up resistance to the aggression, the Patriotic League of Bijeljina put up a four-day resistance, and it was led by Muhidin Bilalic and Haset Tiric, with the remarks that the Patriotic League of Bijeljina had a small numbers of members and modest hunting rifles within its unit. Now, did you know Muhidin Bilalic and Haset Tiric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Haset Tiric I know personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The two of them were commanders of the Muslim forces in Bijeljina, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They weren't the commanders of the Muslim forces in Bijeljina, because there were no Muslim forces in Bijeljina. What there was was citizens, and I'm telling you again, they were the citizens of Bijeljina, citizens. Can you understand the word "citizens of Bijeljina," normal people who were wearing jeans and normal clothing. We never had any insignia or anything like that. We were there, we happened to be there. What you did in Vukovar we wanted to prevent from happening where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, who was in command of you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody. We were there on a spontaneous basis. There was no commander. We were there on a spontaneous basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're a bit fast. Witness, the question is as follows. We have been listening to you. You have explained that in Bijeljina, it was the citizens who set up a defence, and you gave us details. That's very good, but it so happens that a book has been written by a general of the army in your country, and he provided another version in that book, saying that behind it all, there was the Patriotic League. So there's a contradiction between what was said in that book and what you say here, and we were trying to unravel this. Did the general overdo it when he related the events, possibly to glorify the Patriotic League, or is it you failing to underline specific factors, because technically speaking it is difficult to understand that -- if there was a defence, there must have been a leader, there must have been somebody leading the defence, or was everybody a leader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you this way. I've repeated this several times. We citizens gathered together. That means it wasn't organised. There wasn't a commander or anything like that. It was the citizens of Bijeljina. We gathered together. And Karavelic, writing in this book of his, he wasn't in Bijeljina at all. He could just have, well, written this down. He could just write about -- how shall I explain myself, explain this? He could just write what he'd heard, "It is like this, this is what happened," but there wasn't a war going on in Bijeljina for four days, not fighting for four days. As I've already said, they lasted one evening. At about 10.00, they broke out, on the 31st of March, until the 1st in the afternoon, thereabouts, and then that was all. The fighting did not go on for four days, nor was there any Patriotic League, nor did anybody have a uniform or anything else. It was just the citizens that gathered together. So that's what I'm saying. I was there, and then I can tell you what happened. I can repeat this a hundred, a thousand times. I was there on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, are you speaking about the town of Bijeljina or about the municipality of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the town, the town of Bijeljina, the town. I was in town, the town of Bijeljina. Bijeljina is a big municipality as well, including several villages. These villages were around Bijeljina, and most of them were Serb villages; not most of them, 90 per cent. I was born there. I lived there for 27 years up until the conflict broke out. I know every stone in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. You see, the reason I'm asking is to try and sort out this apparent difference between what the ABiH General Karavelic might have to say and what you might have to say about the same incident, and I was trying to figure out if there might have been extended armed action going on outside of the town of Bijeljina. If you say that the fight was only going on for one day in Bijeljina town, then my question to you is: Could it be possible that there were still armed fighting going on outside the town of Bijeljina, but still within the municipality of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fighting could not take place outside of Bijeljina. It wasn't possible, because there were Serb villages around Bijeljina. So from Tuzla, no one could have come. From Brcko, no one could have come to help us. So there wasn't fighting in Brcko. They couldn't even dream that -- well, they couldn't come, they couldn't come, because around Bijeljina there are Serb villages. The only Muslim village was Pejocari [phoen], and it's far from Bijeljina. You have to go through Ugljevik, which is a Serb village. I mean, I would like to explain this, but I can't write a book about what happened in Sarajevo when I was not a Sarajevan myself, or a book about Zenica or whatever. I was in Bijeljina there on that day, on that date, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So the fighting took place only in the town Bijeljina itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The book of Vahid Karavelic is a scholarly work, not a book of memoirs. He's writing about a segment of war from his own ideological and political positions, and he even mentions that they tried to help assistance from the outside to the Muslims in Bijeljina while the fighting went on. And then he says: "During the fighting for Bijeljina, the Patriotic Staff or the Regional Defence of Tuzla took urgent measures to arm and prepare, in an overall fashion, units in Northeastern Bosnia in order to send them to help the defenders of Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "An urgent decision was made to set up three battalions; namely, one in Gradacac, responsible person of Husein Huseinagic, commander of the Patriotic League in Gradacac. He's supposed to help the defenders of Bijeljina through Brezevo Polje to Bijeljina, the 2nd Battalion in the area of Zvornik; responsible person, Sakib Halilovic, commander of the Staff of the Patriotic League from Zvornik. He should be sent to help the defenders of Bijeljina-Zvornik. Janja-Bijeljina is the route they should take. And 3rd Battalion in the area of Zivinice, Said Nistovic was responsible, the then-commander of the regional staff of the Patriotic League of Tuzla, to be sent to assist the defenders of Bijeljina along the Zivinice-Ugljevik-Bijeljina route." As a participant in this conflict, as a defender, as Vahid Karavelic would put it, were you expecting assistance from the outside while the fighting went on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How could we expect assistants when over -- when it is not possible to get there through 10 Serb villages? We didn't have helicopters or planes, so nothing doing, as far as assistance was concerned. And, secondly, we couldn't go on fighting. Why would we fight? Well, I mean, we did fight, but how, why? You had 10 villages. Up to Ugljevik, there are 10 villages. Up to Gradacac, it's 10 Serbian villages. Zvornik, Pilica, you didn't even mention that. Who is going to come, from what side? On the other side is the Drina River in Serbia. From where can we get help? He can write whatever he wants out there. So we were left without any mercy. We were at your mercy. You could kill all of us. We were under a siege, like at the river of Sutjeska. If you know history, you should. You were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was I at Sutjeska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, but you grew up there and you know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is why Vahid Karavelic explains why you did not get assistance in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we have not been provided with text at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "During the preparation of the units on the 2nd of April, 1992, the commander at Gradacac submits a report on readiness to move. However, that same night the units stopped for two reasons. The first was the unit from Gradacac was slowed down by the leadership of Brcko. Then the mayor of Brcko said to the commander of the Tuzla Patriotic League Staff the following: 'I am not going to allow the unit to go through Brcko, because after that the JNA would bomb and level to the ground Brcko itself. Let Bijeljina fend for itself.' I talked to the president, Alija Izetbegovic, and he agreed with my positions." So this is one of the reasons why you did not get help from the battalion in Gradacac. The Muslim president of the municipality of Brcko agreed with Alija Izetbegovic not to let that unit go through Brcko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. No assistance could come in, because already in Brezevo Polje, there were Serb barricades and bunkers and lots of weaponry. There were lots of soldiers in Bre zevo Polje, so they could not get there because of the JNA, was there, the volunteers, the reservists. So around Bijeljina, there were bunkers where the Yugoslav People's Army, volunteers, that is to say, in the direction of Bijeljina from Tuzla, Zvornik, in the direction of Brcko. That is to say, the JNA was there with large groups of soldiers. I told you, we were under siege and we could not get help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since this is a scholarly work written by Vahid Karavelic, so I'm referring to page 237, in footnote number 355 he quotes three sources.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first one is a statement of Alija Muminovic, given to the author himself. The second source is the book of Sefko Hodzic, published in Sarajevo in 1993. And the third source is the Master's paper of Izet Hadzic devoted to this topic, and the Master's degree was obtained at the Faculty of Political Science in Sarajevo in 2001. He quotes these three sources, and are you saying that they are all inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are untrue. I was in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. We are going to move on straight away. You said what you have to say, and we were going to move on. He says the second reason for the lack of success was the delay in the providing of weapons from Sarajevo; namely, the Main Staff of the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina promised for a long time that ammunition and weapons would come in, in February and March. And then when the Regional Staff of the Patriotic League in Tuzla established units to help Bijeljina, it was stated that on the 2nd of April, 1992, weapons would arrive in Zivinice. However, just like until then, on that occasion, too, weapons did not arrive. Only a few days later, the Regional Staff of the Patriotic League of Tuzla -- and so on. This doesn't really matter for our purposes. That was already late when you lost the battle for Bijeljina. He mentions as a second reason the delay in providing weapons, and they couldn't arm these three battalions. Do you find that strange, what is written in his book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I find it strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Just another quotation from his book, page 241.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "After the telephone report of the commander of the Patriotic League of Bijeljina on the 4th of April, 1992, concerning the situation in Bijeljina, the units of the Patriotic League and part of the population of Bijeljina that wished to get out with permission of the commander of the Regional Staff of the Patriotic League of Tuzla, they started getting out in the direction of Brcko and Tuzla, and after that Bijeljina was occupied." So that is to say that you had enough strength to withdraw in the direction of Brcko and Tuzla in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true. I already told you, we, the young men who were on the barricades, we left individually, just like I left and went to a third country, so that's not true. A young man was killed on the barricades when he tried to pass through the Serb forces on foot. Never mind you killed him. A bird could not fly over anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. This is what he says here: "After the occupation of Bijeljina, part of the units of the Patriotic League, headed by Haset Tiric, was withdrawing through Teocak and Tuzla in the area, in the direction of Zivinice, where the expelled Regional Staff of the Patriotic Staff was at the time. "Later on, they were renamed, whereas Muris Ibrahimovic and another group managed to get to the area of Brcko." On the base of this, it would seem that you were in this group led by Muris Ibrahimovic and managed to get to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Go ahead, finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came on a bus. My colleague and I went on a bus. A colleague who was not in the barricades at all, a regular guy. We passed through on a bus, and on that day in Brezevo Polje, there were no checks. If there were checks, I wouldn't be here today, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. In footnote 365, he quotes several documents that are in the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the official name of your army; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the army later, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we have what Vahid Karavelic says. Now let us look at some other matters. Over here, you mentioned fighting in Bijeljina, and you said that in Bijeljina, there was the JNA, the reservists, the volunteers of Mirko Blagojevic, and Arkan's men, right; and you called Mirko Blagojevic's volunteers "Seselj's men"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was the Radical Party, and you're the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I am the president.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And who does Mirko Blagojevic belong to? He is yours; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, he's my closest friend and party associate, the president of our party for Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So am I lying?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: About that? No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never lied anyway. I'm from a family --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But what you said about the killing of the Muslims, you invented all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Witness and Mr. Seselj, you are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that among the volunteers that you call "Seselj's men," and I'm proud of the fact that you're calling them "Seselj's men," the volunteers led by Mirko Blagojevic, was there anyone from Serbia among them? Was there anyone who wasn't from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From Serbia, it was only Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arkan's men were from Serbia for the most part, but there was this one man from Bijeljina there too. I know him. He's younger than I am. He went to my elementary school. I couldn't -- I could recognise him, but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have too much time left. How much time do I have left? Could you tell me so that I can see what I could deal with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Empirically, I believe you have about 20 minutes left, but Mr. Registrar is going to confirm this. I was wrong by two minutes. You have 18 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I hope that I will manage to deal with important things, at least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, could I have a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a break. Let's have a 20-minute break, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in session. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have some information about crimes which according to your testimony were perpetrated by Arkan's men, when the photographs were shown. Now, do you know of any specific piece of information to which Mirko Blagojevic and his men committed any crimes during the battle of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know a piece of information to this effect: That Mirko Blagojevic killed -- perhaps killed -- well, 100 per cent -- well, he didn't kill, but he ordered the killing of Nargalic, Coso Nargalic. The other one, the other piece of information is this. My professor, Ferid Zecevic, was proclaimed by you, by the Radical Party and Mirko Blagojevic that he's some kind of Mujahedin, that he's some kind of Islamic army or whatever and that he organised something. Because of that I consider that he either ordered or gave a statement -- or made a statement that he should be done away with, killed. I think that that was in Batkovic camp. That's my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. What can Mirko Blagojevic have to do with the camp in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because nobody knew of Arkan's men 100 per cent. Well, I considered that nobody knew that Ferid Zecevic was some kind of organiser of the Islamic Mujahedin or -- or Coso, because in the past, before the war, Coso and Blagojevic had verbal duals, because Coso was a boxer and Blagojevic was a boxer; and so they had conflicts and clashes, which means that 100 per cent certain Blagojevic is responsible for Coso's death. I don't know who killed Coso Nargalic, but I know he wielded influence on that killing, which means that Arkan's men didn't know who Nargalic was or who Ferid Zecevic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you're just making assumptions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I think I'm 90 per cent correct that that's how it was, and that's what I'm saying, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You think that that's how it was, but you haven't got a shred of evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have a piece of evidence. When we were at the barricades, Cazim passed by us, Cazim Karadzic, the former colleague -- a former colleague of Mirko Blagojevic. He had been beaten up. He was covered in blood, and we could hardly recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So all those are your assumptions, speculation on your part. You don't know anything for sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cazim Karadzic was beaten up. I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who beat him up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko's men, Mirko Blagojevic's men beat him up, Cazim Karadzic. I repeat once again. That means he was beaten up, they beat him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was Cazim Karadzic beaten up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening. I don't know where he happened to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the following day, the 1st of March. That's when he was beaten up. He passed by us, and we couldn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say the 1st of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I meant the 1st of April. After the conflicts in the evening, when we set up the barricades, he passed by us that same day, and I couldn't recognise the man. I knew him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's stop. Pause there for a bit. Did he tell you that Mirko Blagojevic's men had beaten him up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Mirko Blagojevic said he was in a hotel where he had been beaten up. Mirko Blagojevic happened to be in the hotel where he was beaten up, and he said, "What have they done to you, Cazim," that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So Mirko said to him, "What have they done to you, Cazim"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And from that, you draw the conclusion that Mirko's men beat him up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, come on, come on, let's move on. If you find that normal and natural, let's move on straight away. Now, do you know that the Serbian Radical Party in Bijeljina was established together by Mirko Blagojevic and Izet Salihbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Izet Salihbegovic and his late brother, the brother who died and was the proprietor of a cafe opposite the park. I know them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you know that he and Mirko set up the party together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, because I'm not interested in the man at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Then we can move on right away. Now, you said in your statement somewhere that in the Srbija Cafe, Arkan's men, Captain Dragan's men, congregated and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't put it that way. I said that Serbs frequented the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, when did Arkan arrive in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 15 days before, he was seen around Bijeljina with his unit as he was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how many men did his units number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They appeared in those military "pinskalas" [phoen] or what are they called?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've just invented that, made it all up, and wait for me to ask you the question. Arkan first appeared in Bijeljina in the early-morning hours of the 1st of April, 1992, and he arrived with 29 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct. Arkan's men and that young man whom I knew came earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who called Arkan to come to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who called him, but I do know that he was in Bijeljina before --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I tell you that he was called personally by Biljana Plavsic, does that tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that immediately after the liberation of Bijeljina, Biljana Plavsic arrived with Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was disloyal, a traitor to his people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic is not important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is important. You could say that Fikret Abdic came to Bijeljina, which means he was a traitor of his own people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and speak one at a time. They are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, refrain from proclaiming people traitors, will you, because you, from Brcko, fled to Western Europe. It never occurred to you to fight in the war. Now let's see this: Do you know that Biljana Plavsic, immediately upon arrival in Bijeljina, publicly kissed Arkan? That was public, it was on television.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Biljana Plavsic struck a bargain with The Hague Tribunal to be given a smaller sentence, and that she appeared as a false witness in the Momcilo Krajisnik trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We'll move on. Does the name of Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You killed him after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you Serbs, your own people, not my people. Mauzer was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you sorry that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. You would have to ask that question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, why would it be important for us here who killed Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just asked you whether his name was familiar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Mauzer took part in the fighting in Bijeljina too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Mauzer, after those battles, in cooperation with Arkan, set up the guards that were called the Panthers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, because I wasn't in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, do you know this: that Mauzer, immediately after the liberation of Bijeljina, took over -- seized power, almost all power, in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that, and I'd heard you killed him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. The fact that we killed him later on, well, that's not it. Well, maybe it's a good idea, maybe it's not. But why is that important, that Mauzer was killed later? Let's focus on my questions. What do I care that Mauzer was killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please try and wait with your answer until you have seen the cursor on the screen in front of you stop, because only when the cursor stops is the translation finished. You see, if you overlap, then we do not understand a word of what you're saying, and then we might as well just close.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a man from Bijeljina, although you weren't present yourself, do you know, in talking to other fellow townsmen, that after these battles, Mauzer ceased to respect any military and political authority in Republika Srpska, that he set out on his own, he became independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do know that, and perhaps he was right in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You can continue to support him and say he was right in doing so, but what I'm asking you is this: Do you know that Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic avoided coming to Bijeljina while Mauzer was the main authority there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Mirko Blagojevic and the Serbian Radical Party were for years in a public conflict with Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, do you know this: that Mauzer, in addition to closely cooperating with Arkan, was the vice-president of the Democratic Party of Zoran Djindjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that after the Dayton Accords, he went out to the elections in Republika Srpska at the head of Djindjic's Democratic Party for Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that means that the man was in favour of democracy, which means he was a good man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you go on commending him. It's very nice of you to do so. Now, do you know that after those elections, Mauzer became the main chief of police in Republika Srpska, the deputy to the minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. Can I tell you something? I'm not interested in Mauzer at all. I'm not interested in the topic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, many books published by the Muslims, your compatriots, I find the information that main crimes against the Bijeljina Muslims were perpetrated by Arkan and Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you go ahead and defend Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not defending Mauzer. All I'm saying is this: If he was in the Democratic Party of Zoran Djindjic, it means he was repentant and that he had opted for democracy. That's all I said. I didn't say I defended him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he continued in his mafia dealings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me say again --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who looted the whole of Janja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Janja is the largest Muslim village in Bijeljina municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. Between Janja and Bijeljina, there are 10 Serb villages, and between Janja and Zvornik too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how are you, as a Muslim, not interested in who looted the whole of Janja and expelled the whole of the Muslim population from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I know who was expelled from Bijeljina, who expelled the Muslims from Bijeljina and Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- just a moment, just let me remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it somebody who was a self-appointed major, perhaps? Was his name similar to mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, just let me take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew his name, but I can't remember it just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it Vojkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Vojkan. He expelled my mother. My mother was on the list too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was his surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Djuric. It began with a "Dj" letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean Djurkovic. Do you know Mirko Blagojevic was in conflict with him all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that Mirko Blagojevic from the very first day fought against the expulsion and persecution of Muslims from the Bijeljina area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, The Hague Tribunal has public statements made by Mirko Blagojevic in standing up to Mauzer and Djurkovic and I have copies of that here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did stand up to them, but finally he said that we should all be expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Mirko Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've just invented that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping, and it is impossible to interpret. Could they please slow one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the OTP people talked to you and proofed you, led by Mr. Mussemeyer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, take your time. You are speaking too fast, responding too fast, and the interpreters are complaining once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the proofing session, did Mr. Mussemeyer perhaps show you the public statements made in 1992 and 1993, and the following years, by Mirko Blagojevic in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993, well, that was already the area where there were no more Muslims left. I think there was just a small percentage. So the important day is the 31st and the 1st and after that, whereas in 1993, there were no more Muslims there, so whom could he have protected? To protect Muslims, the Muslims had to go up to the line and dig trenches for the Serb forces up at Mount Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were enough Muslims in Bijeljina, and some of them were members of the Serbian army, and Mauzer expelled those, too, from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, if you say it's not true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not true. They had to go and dig trenches. They were forced to go and dig trenches at Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that Mr. Mussemeyer didn't show you the public statements made by Mirko Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what Mirko Blagojevic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you about the Prosecutor, Mr. Mussemeyer. He's over there, across the way, sitting in the courtroom. He conducted the proofing session with you. Well, if he didn't show you that, he didn't prepare you for this -- for your testimony well enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I prepared myself, and I'm saying what I said, what I've already said. I've talked about it, and that's what I want to talk about. I don't want to talk about Mauzer and what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You seem to me to be a little nervous. You're too nervous during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are swerving from the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, don't fly off the handle. It's useless.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Comrade Judge, he's talking about subjects that I'm not interested in. I'm focusing on my own topic, so he should speak about what I said, not about Mauzer, because when I left Bijeljina, I wasn't interested about what happened afterwards, whether Mirko Blagojevic, in 1993, was saving the Muslims or whether he was persecuting them. I focused my attention from the 31st and the 1st. Well, I wasn't interested in Mauzer at all, nor was I interested in Vojkan Djurkovic. He's on the list. My mother was expelled, too. She was on the list, and that was in the Bosnian papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj is interested in this. If you don't have the answer, just say, "I don't know." That's it. Unfortunately, you cannot choose the questions that are going to be put to you, the questions that you want to answer. You must answer all questions put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you only know one thing, what you've invented; that I was sitting in the cafe, up at the bar, with Mirko Blagojevic, deciding on the killing of the Muslims, and on the basis of that you seem to have merited that The Hague Tribunal has managed to procure a residency for you in a foreign country. So that's all you're sticking to. You're not interested in anything else. You weren't interested in the struggle and fight of the Muslims, although you took part a little bit in the first days. Then you beat a hasty retreat from Brcko to the West, and you weren't interested anymore. And now you've come to fulfill what you owe The Hague Tribunal as a mark of recognition and gratitude for them having got you a permit in a foreign country, where you have a good job and a good salary and you couldn't care less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can say whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Judge, Your Honour, I want to say this: What I said here is the truth. Secondly, you can take it -- well, you can take documents from the police in the country in which I'm residing, when you know on the basis of which I was granted a residence permit. So I don't need to give anything back to The Hague Tribunal that I owe them. I obtained my papers in regular fashion through my wife. I am legally married to my wife, and it was through her that I was able to get my papers. I state once again that what Mr. Seselj is saying is not the truth. So whenever you want to see the documents, my file in the police station, on the basis of which I was granted a residency permit. So let me repeat that once again. That's why I'm nervous, because of his lies, because he is not telling the truth. So he does not know how I came to be given my residency papers, so I ask you once again to take my police file, look at the documents, and then we can resolve that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You received your papers on the basis of a number of requests made by The Hague Tribunal to the state organs of that country, and of those many requests, one of them has been provided by Mr. Mussemeyer, and it is Patrick Lopez-Terres' letter three days after talking to you and after you had signed the statement. Immediate -- he reacted immediately to protect you as a valuable witness; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what does this paper mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the paper, but it wasn't on the basis of that paper that I was given residency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is this a forgery, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) documents referring to the request made by The Hague Tribunal and the OTP of The Hague. Now, Judges, Mr. Mussemeyer should have brought in the document from 2007 granting this witness permanent residence in the third country. We're lacking a lot of documents, but we do have 11 pages that are very valuable and explain everything to us. So this isn't documentation against this witness, primarily; it is against The Hague OTP and the methods employed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we need to redact line 5, page 98. There is mention of the country. Line 5, page 98. I believe your time has almost run out, Mr. Seselj. Please resume and finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I mention the country? I don't think I did. I mentioned it? Well, then it was truly by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1028, the price that you paid in order to get permanent residency is not a high one in your moral framework, but in the moral framework that all honest people are guided by and all of mankind is guided by, it is a very, very high price. It's better not to be alive than to perjure oneself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your people and in your religious group, perjury is one of the most terrible crimes, whereas you decided to perjure yourself in order to get a residency permit. We have information attesting to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I say something now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I realise the accused now is changing from using the words "false witness." He is using other words, but the meaning is the same. He should restrain from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what do you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that what he said, I mean, that I got papers on the basis of the fact that I came here, that's not true. You can check that. You can check that. I've said that several times. I didn't get papers on that basis, nor would I ask to get papers on that basis. As for my faith, I am very clear on that. I never lied. I come from a very good family, too. I'm not interested in his faith, but what I say, that is true. You can take the documentation from the police of the country that I am in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for you in this respect. Based on the documents that we have been given, or based on this document, you went to the country I'm not going to name on the 11th of May, 1992, and you applied for asylum. The application was denied. And based on this document, you then left the country in question. Later on, you returned to that country, and at some point I see this detail in the document: On the 23rd of November, 1999, you explained to an office in that country that you have not left the country. On the 14th of November, 2000, so that's one year later, you introduced or presented a passport, and you allegedly gave your real name then. Does this mean that when you went to that country, you went under a fake name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I used a different name, because they were looking for me. In 1992, when I came to this country where I had been, a woman told me -- a woman who was there told me that she had heard that I had already been killed, that I was no longer among the living, so I had to protect my life. I had to say something. So since in that country, on that year, it wasn't that only Muslims had fled; Serbs and Croats had sought refuge there too. Many Serbs assumed Muslim names in order to register. So I had to protect myself somehow, so for the sake of my own safety and security, I had to change my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, sir, you applied in 1992 for asylum, and it was a regular application. No problem about that. But later on, in 1995, you returned to that country. Then, obviously, you gave a different name, and you applied for asylum under a different name, and that's the reality of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already explained, I was afraid. I was afraid for my life. I feared for my life, and I explained that to the police of that country, and it says that over there. So it was for the sake of my own safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have only two additional questions. But before I come to this, I must again make you aware that the accused has used extensively a book which he did not provide before cross-examination. He even did not inform us that he would quote from this book. And for me, this is completely unprofessional. Now to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know the date, the month, for example, when you got the permanent residence in the country you are living in now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, 2007. I think that was it, the 25th of May, 2007. The 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And the second statement you gave to us was in November of 2007, so that was some months after you got the permanent residence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: My second question: Which month in 1992 did you leave Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in April, mid-April, after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Just to assist the Trial Chamber, the letter Mr. Seselj was referring to, the letter from Mr. Blagojevic, is from September, the 27th of September, 1992. So the witness has already left in April and Mr. Blagojevic wrote this letter in September. It has the exhibit number -- not the exhibit number, sorry, the 65 ter number 1677 and 1678. It's the same document. This is all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. This concludes your testimony, Witness. I shall ask the usher -- he is not there because he had to take a document out of the courtroom. Before you leave the courtroom, we have to lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something at the end now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that what I testified here against Mr. Seselj, I mean, I would like to say that all Serbs or other ethnicities -- well, I really don't know how to put this. I mean, not everybody is the same. And may I also say that I hope that the evil that befell my people and my country never befall anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're going to be escorted out of the courtroom, but first the usher has to lower the blinds. You may leave the courtroom. Let's make sure that the cameras are not turned on. Let's move into private session before you leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow, in open session, we'll have Witness VS-44. Of course, since he's a Court witness, a witness of the Trial Chamber, I'll ask him whether he wants to testify in open session, and thereafter the Trial Chamber will have questions for the witness. As usual, I can already sketch out the proceedings: that everybody be prepared; there will be questions on his personal situation; his political involvement in the 1990s; then he will be asked questions regarding the Serb Radical Party from 1991 to 1994; then the issue of dispatching volunteers; relationships between Mr. Seselj and other members of the joint criminal enterprise; questions on speeches made by Mr. Seselj; the issue of financing of the SRS; questions on the part played within the SRS by Mr. Seselj; and other questions arising from the usual questions. Once that is over, the Prosecutor will have an hour, Mr. Seselj too. But since the Judges are basically going to cover the entire scope of all these questions, it may be that you just have residual questions to put, inasmuch as the Trial Chamber will deal with the essential questions during that first stage of the proceedings. We shall endeavour to comply with the schedule in the hope that we can finish tomorrow's hearing with the testimony of this witness. Let us hope that he will arrive today. He was supposed to arrive today, and since he's a witness of the Trial Chamber, nobody will see him before he gets to this courtroom; neither the Judges, nor the Prosecution or the accused. The time has come for us to adjourn. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 8.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of December, 2008, at 8.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.52 p.m.,
